title: When a stranger goes in for a kiss
subtitle: The "no gracias" hat isn't working
content:
Travelling: 100% guaranteed to meet people

After one hour biking along the coastal cliffs of Lima, I locked up my rental outside a small café in Barranco to grab a coffee. A man named Claudio, waiting for the same table, struck up a conversation in a mix of English and Spanish. We ended up talking for almost an hour — about his work, my trip, the neighbourhood.

When it was time to go, we walked together up some stairs surrounded by bright, gorgeous mural art — and that's when he leaned in for a kiss. I turned my head so it landed on my cheek instead, laughed it off, and said my goodbyes. The "no gracias" cap, it turns out, does not actually communicate "no gracias" to everyone.

Feelings check

I'm still working through some anxiety about leaving my accommodation alone, even for small errands. It helps that I've become a little obsessed with ordering food straight to where I'm staying instead of forcing myself out every time.

Meeting Claudio was a nice reminder that most interactions on the road are warm, easy ones — even the slightly awkward ones. My social battery runs out fast, but moments like today make the harder days worth it.

where I stayed

Accommodation review

Cute, cozy, clean and centrally located apartment that's quiet when the windows are closed.

title: When the best laid plans fail
subtitle: And it's okay to turn back!
content:
How [not] to prepare for 5 months of hiking

  1. Stay home
  2. Lounge in the sun
  3. Smoke weed
  4. Eat chocolate
  5. Snuggle your cat (or dog, pillow, spouse)

Usually one may consider hitting the gym, regularly running or doing practice hikes at high altitude but I wanted to counteract the active lifestyle I was about to have with an opposite one filled with comfort and mostly sedentary activities.

I was pretty certain becoming active again would be like riding a bike. Of course a lack of appetite without marijuana and high altitude would slow me down but in time, I can do anything! Right?

So on my last day in Mexico City, I scheduled three Ubers to make one volcanic hike happen.

  • The first car would pick me up early in the morning to take me 1 hour to the Ajusco Peak trail head.
  • The second would come when the hike was over, taking me back to my accommodation.
  • The third would bring me to the airport once I clean up and repack.

I gave myself 7.5 hours to do a hard 6 KM loop before flying to Peru at 10 PM that same evening.

The blisters I sustained from walking over 25 K steps in the city two days prior were bandaged. I even had snacks and cash for the park.

I felt well prepared, even double checking the location of the restaurant I was using for the Uber drop off and pick up after learning there were two on opposite sides of the city.

So, with the help of a natural sleep aid, it was early to bed before catching the first car.

When I got out of the Uber on what seemed to be the side of a major motorway, I sat in Cabana Vicky's about to order food when I noticed Alltrails said I was an 11 hour walk away…

What?

Sorry, WHAT???

How?

I put in the wrong Cabana Vicky's…. There are two, maybe more.

Feeling the clock ticking down, I ordered another Uber to take me to the correct location immediately and ate a packed snack in the shade while waiting.

It would be another 60 minute drive to where I wanted to go, meaning now I'd only have 6 or so hours to complete the hike before my flight.

I can still do this.

The Mexico City traffic was in full force now and the roads near the end were so steep I didn't think the manual car would make it up. Cellular service was minimal and following any map app became unreliable. I have to think that is why the driver stopped and let me out somewhere that was still an 18 minute drive away from where I wanted to be.

So I ordered a third Uber to take me the rest of the way, slightly panicking about only now having 5 or so hours to complete the hike.

I was dropped off in the middle of nowhere, about a 5 minute walk away from the trailhead. There was a low wooden gate topped with barbed wire in front of a trail that I could see on my offline map connected to where I wanted to be.

So I hopped the fence and started my hike! I was pretty much gassed immediately because of the high altitude but assumed I'd adjust quickly.

The trail disappeared after a few minutes into overgrown brush so I was forced back onto the road, now covered in greenery and thankful for the immediate break from walking upwards.

Minutes later, I FINALLY ended up at the official front gate where you sign in and pay for the hike. Not many people were on the trail and no one was hiking solo.

I had barely started moving before having thoughts about turning around.

That is unlike me.

Plus the sunk cost of all those Ubers was weighing on me.

So with a carrot in hand to munch on for energy, I climbed.

Everyone 100 meters I must have stopped to catch my breath. I couldn't even distract myself with music, podcasts, audiobooks or the beauty of nature. Breathing was so hard!

I could see from my map that it was only 3 KM up before a leisurely walk down but after less than 1 KM, I had to recalculate.

So I found a nice rock to enjoy the view from before turning back.

I reasoned that the higher I went, the foggier it would be so it's not like I was going to get a better view from the top than what I had from where I was. I also wasn't confident the Uber I scheduled to pick me up from that barbed wire fence would actually arrive given the lack of cellular service and I did not want to risk missing my flight or being rushed to repack.

A couple passed me on my break and we chatted briefly about where I was from and my plan to go back down.

I saw them later in the parking lot and they offered to take me into the nearest town where I'd have service to order an Uber to take me home.

Thank you Marco from Mexico and Daddi from Cuba!

I was grateful that the park employees also offered to drive me into cellular service and thought this must happen a lot to tourists.

Feelings check

Of course I felt a little silly for messing up the Uber drop offs multiple times. I know I haven't been eating enough so my mind and patience are not at their best. I was humbled by not being able to complete the hike and surprised at my lack of motivation to persevere. This experience worries me for my plans to complete future high altitude hikes.

I was extremely burnt out from all the car rides and couldn't bring myself to go out for food after arriving back from the hike and before heading to the airport.

Napping felt natural but the dogs barking incessantly prevented that from happening for long.

On the bright side, the Popocatépetl volcano was very active before sunset and despite the noise keeping me awake, it was incredible to watch.

Balanced reflections

Joy
  • Affordable Ubers able to take me to random places so I never feel stranded
  • Watching volcanic activity from the privacy of my balcony
Pain
  • Having shortness of breath while hiking at 3500 meters
  • Not being well fed makes my temper short and my nervous system unable to deal with noise

where I stayed

Accommodation review

The view was exceptional but all things considered, I probably wouldn't stay again.

Bed

Cozy against the wall with the flannel sheets and a variety of 3 pillows.

Space

Small and functional with lots of big windows and bright yellow curtains.

Views

Incredible to see multiple volcanos, the sprawling city and many Mexican flags.

Neighbourhood

Seemingly unknown by locals with lots of cute streets, mural art, stores and shops.

Noise

Loud with dogs barking, neighbours talking, people broadcasting and construction.

Host-pitality

Didn't meet and no local advice was given but communication was reasonable.

Privacy

None on the balcony due to neighbours, but lots if the curtains are closed.

Value

Not great given a lack of wifi out in the area and not enough tea or toilet paper.

Getting around

All necessities in walking distance and Ubers are affordable to get into the city.

Cleanliness

A few small bugs given there are no screens and stray hairs, but otherwise clean.

title: Practico español
subtitle: Ordering food and drink
content:
After 930 days on duo lingo…

It's finally time to use what Spanish I've learned online in the real world. The uber driver didn't have much to say on the way here but I've been chatting with my accommodation hosts and writing my daily journals en Español. Plus there is Netflix with Spanish subtitles.

I felt pretty confident ordering pollo enchiladas until they asked if I wanted a beverage and then brought me the largest michelada I've ever handled. After a few sips, I was tipsy and full. Thankfully you can take anything to-go in Mexico, even alcohol.

When I couldn't pay, one of the employees offered to walk me to an ATM. That was a great opportunity to speak Spanish despite not being able to take out any cash. Luckily I was able to transfer him money for the meal. I asked him if he'd always lived here and he said yes but would like to visit Amsterdam. Of course then I had to ask him about marijuana and he told me he also likes LSD. I told him about the molly bears I brought and that this was the first day of my 5 month trip to practice Spanish in South America :)

During the quick walk back to my place, a family in a car stopped me to ask where I had gotten the take out and beverage I was carrying. Unfortunately I was caught off guard and the traffic pressure did not allow me to respond helpfully.

Feelings check

I felt uneasy waking up in Mexico City for the first full day of 5 months away from home. I was nervous to leave my booking.com accommodation because of the masking required to interact even minimally with the public.

I know it's obvious that I'm not from here and I need to be extra vigilant and safe with information I give out.

The neighbourhood where I'm staying is hilly, filled with graffiti murals and small shops that only accept cash. There are so many volcanic peaks dotting the landscape of the view from my apartment and a lot of trails to explore. It feels overwhelming not to be able to see the entire city and each national park in the less than 10 days I will be spending here.

It still doesn't feel real that my adventure has begun. I'm not sure when that will change. I think starting with a low pressure rest day was smart. I wasn't ready for a full day out walking so soon.

I'll probably be hungover tomorrow!

Balanced reflections

Joy?
  • Daniel sending me polos and staying in touch via text, telling me he misses me, Hulky and him enjoying my balcony before the renter comes
  • Those first few sips of alcohol and talking to my Oma live at the restaurant I was eating at
Pain?
  • Physically my neck feels a bit stiff
  • Reminders of my time dating Jael and us meeting in Mexico. It doesn't help that he's messaging me, sending voice notes, calling me baby and trying to make plans to see me in February here

title: 5 months trekking through South America
subtitle: Solo travelling with a personal item sized bag
content:
With research and experimentation, you can pack less!

Almost every year I plan 3 or 4 month long adventures to explore remote trails around the world and I'm taking off soon on my longest trip yet, 5 months!

When a carry-on sized item was included in most economy tickets, I'd take my favourite pastel roller bag onto the planes, a backpack and a pillow case stuffed with extra clothing. Now that base fares only include a personal sized item, I'll be taking just a small backpack, fanny pack and neck pillow case stuffed with smaller items.

What you decide to bring depends on where you're going, the climate and weather, what you'll be doing and your personal preferences. I've packed and repacked almost 20 times in the last 3 months, narrowing down my must-haves for trekking in South America — see the full pack list and rationale.

The benefits of travelling with JUST a personal item sized bag include:

  1. Avoiding airline baggage fees
  2. Saving time at the airport
  3. Zero lost bag anxiety
  4. Reducing daily decision fatigue
  5. Appearing less touristy

I went for a bag that would fit in the smallest of budget airline baggage sizers and that would hold its shape when fully loaded, the Sherpani Soleil. Light material like merino wool reduces the overall weight of the bag, as does holding heavier items like battery packs in a fanny pack or on your person in some other way. I try to avoid packing liquids for the same reason.

No matter what, the only shoes you can bring are the ones on your feet! I'm obsessed with Hoka's Hopara line of all purpose hiking shoes. They're waterproof and I've run, walked endlessly and summited mountains in them.

All of this already feels like an accomplishment and I can't wait to see if I've made all the right decisions or what I'd change for next time. Was every item packed used? Did the compression bag hold up? Was it possible to remain organized?

Feelings check

Only 10 days before I'll be falling asleep in Mexico City, starting several adventures of a lifetime again. On the one hand, 5 months feels unfathomable. On the other hand, I know it's going to fly by and I'll be back to my vibrator and weed in no time. Coming back to essential oil diffusers, warm baths, Lenige lip masks and Aesop hand cream are experiences I will greatly anticipate upon return. Not to mention snuggling my cat again when she comes back for my birthday month and the opening of my balcony space with the sun's return to it.

Life is good. I am lucky. This is so many dreams come true and my ideal lifestyle. I'm not employed but it's a gift to be in this millennial pause or mid-career retirement, whatever you want to call it, while I have the good health and energy to see more of the beautiful world. I have to believe what's meant to happen will and that I am making all the right moves to reveal my future opportunities.

From the written journal:
